items.prompt: What is a "pull request (PR)"?
choices: A proposed change, presented for review and automated checks before it's merged into the shared branch
A request sent to a database to pull the latest records
A command that downloads a repository for the first time
A formal complaint filed about a teammate's code
items.explanation: A PR is a checkpoint — a proposed change that gets scrutinized (by both automated checks and humans) before it becomes part of the shared branch everyone builds on.
items.reference:
📝 PR — a proposed change, not yet merged
🔍 Checkpoint — reviewed and checked before it affects everyone

Why: the value of a PR is entirely in what happens before merge, not the merge itself.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of a PR, beyond just moving code into the shared branch?
choices: It's a checkpoint where automated checks and human review both get applied before the change becomes everyone's problem
It exists purely to create a permanent historical record with no functional purpose
It automatically fixes any bugs in the proposed code
It replaces the need for any commit messages
items.explanation: A PR's value is the scrutiny applied before the change lands — treating it as just a mechanical step to get code merged misses why it exists.
items.reference:
📝 PR — a proposed change, not yet merged
🔍 Checkpoint — reviewed and checked before it affects everyone

Why: the value of a PR is entirely in what happens before merge, not the merge itself.

items.prompt: What is "CI (continuous integration) gating"?
choices: Configuring the shared branch so a PR literally cannot merge until its automated checks pass
A tool that automatically writes code review comments
A meeting held before every merge to discuss the change
A setting that prevents any PR from ever being opened
items.explanation: CI gating turns "please run the tests" into an enforced requirement — the merge button itself is disabled until checks pass, not just discouraged.
items.reference:
🚧 Gating — merge button disabled until checks pass
🙏 Not gating — a request that depends on someone remembering

Why: a request that depends on memory under deadline pressure eventually gets skipped — gating removes that choice entirely.

items.prompt: Why does CI gating matter more than just asking engineers to run tests before merging?
choices: A request that depends on someone remembering, under deadline pressure, eventually gets skipped — gating removes that decision entirely
Because engineers are incapable of running tests manually
Because gating makes tests run faster
Because gating is required by version control software to function at all
items.explanation: "I'm confident this is fine" is always available as a justification under pressure — a blocking gate removes the need to trust that justification.
items.reference:
🚧 Gating — merge button disabled until checks pass
🙏 Not gating — a request that depends on someone remembering

Why: a request that depends on memory under deadline pressure eventually gets skipped — gating removes that choice entirely.

items.prompt: What is "review culture," as this unit defines it?
choices: The shared norms around what reviewers actually check for and how feedback is given
A mandatory training course all new engineers must complete
The specific software used to display code diffs
A rule requiring at least three reviewers per PR
items.explanation: Review culture is about what reviewers actually do in practice — whether review means genuine engagement or a rubber stamp — not any specific tool or headcount rule.
items.reference:
✅ Real review culture — engaging with what changed and why
❌ Rubber-stamp culture — skim and approve

Why: the same PR process can produce very different outcomes depending entirely on this norm.

items.prompt: How does "review culture" differ between a team that treats review as genuine engagement versus one that treats it as a formality?
choices: The team that engages genuinely actually catches the untested-scenario category of bug; the rubber-stamp team gets none of review's real value despite having the same process
There is no meaningful difference — both produce identical outcomes
The rubber-stamp team merges code faster with no downsides
Genuine engagement is only possible with more than five reviewers
items.explanation: The PR process can look identical on paper while producing very different real outcomes, depending entirely on whether reviewers actually engage with the diff.
items.reference:
✅ Real review culture — engaging with what changed and why
❌ Rubber-stamp culture — skim and approve

Why: the same PR process can produce very different outcomes depending entirely on this norm.

items.prompt: What is a "blocking check"?
choices: An automated check configured to prevent a merge on failure, as opposed to one that only reports a warning
A check that runs only once per week
A manual step where a senior engineer personally approves every merge
A check that blocks a specific engineer from ever merging code
items.explanation: A blocking check physically prevents the merge until it passes — a non-blocking check might still report failures but doesn't stop anything.
items.reference:
🚫 Blocking — merge literally cannot proceed on failure
⚠️ Non-blocking — reports a warning, merge proceeds anyway

Why: a non-blocking check that's meant to function like a blocking one will eventually be ignored under time pressure.

items.prompt: What happens if a check is configured as non-blocking "just for visibility," but the team expects it to function like a real gate?
choices: It will eventually be overridden or ignored under time pressure, since the whole point of gating is removing that choice
Nothing changes — non-blocking and blocking checks behave identically
The check automatically becomes blocking after a few uses
The merge button disables itself regardless of the check's configuration
items.explanation: A check that can be overridden will be, eventually — expecting non-blocking configuration to produce blocking-check discipline is a real, common failure mode.
items.reference:
🚫 Blocking — merge literally cannot proceed on failure
⚠️ Non-blocking — reports a warning, merge proceeds anyway

Why: a non-blocking check that's meant to function like a blocking one will eventually be ignored under time pressure.

items.prompt: What is "diff review"?
choices: Reading the actual lines that changed (and the reasoning behind them), as opposed to just trusting a green checkmark
A tool that automatically summarizes every PR in one sentence
The process of comparing two different programming languages
A check that verifies the PR's title matches a specific format
items.explanation: Diff review means actually engaging with the specific lines that changed — the human half of a PR's scrutiny, distinct from re-trusting automated results.
items.reference:
👀 Diff review — reading the actual changed lines and reasoning
✅ Not diff review — just re-checking that CI passed

Why: this is the specific activity that catches the untested-scenario category of bug from the opening scenario.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, what did the reviewer do that counts as "diff review"?
choices: Read the new discount-combining function and asked what happens if the combined discount goes over 100%
Re-ran the existing test suite and confirmed it passed
Checked that the PR's title followed the team's naming convention
Approved the PR without opening it
items.explanation: The reviewer engaged with the actual new logic and asked a substantive question about its behavior — exactly what diff review means in practice, distinct from re-confirming CI's result.
items.reference:
👀 Diff review — reading the actual changed lines and reasoning
✅ Not diff review — just re-checking that CI passed

Why: this is the specific activity that catches the untested-scenario category of bug from the opening scenario.

items.prompt: In the opening scenario, why did every existing test pass on the buggy PR?
choices: None of the existing tests happened to combine a member discount with a coupon, so the over-100% scenario was never tested
The tests were poorly written and contained bugs of their own
CI was misconfigured and skipped running some tests
The reviewer had already fixed the bug before CI ran
items.explanation: The existing suite tested real, valid scenarios correctly — the combined-discount scenario simply didn't exist as a possibility until this PR introduced it, so nothing had ever tested it.
items.reference:
✅ CI — every existing test passes
🙋 Reviewer's question — "what if the discounts stack past 100%?"
💸 Answer — the price goes negative

Why: this is the entire mechanism the unit explains — CI can only check what's already been thought to test.

items.prompt: What question did the reviewer ask that CI structurally could not have asked on its own?
choices: "What happens if the combined discount goes over 100%?"
"Did all the tests pass?"
"Is the code formatted correctly?"
"How long did the build take?"
items.explanation: This question requires reasoning about a scenario nobody had encoded as a test yet — exactly the category of question only a human reviewer reading the actual logic can ask.
items.reference:
✅ CI — every existing test passes
🙋 Reviewer's question — "what if the discounts stack past 100%?"
💸 Answer — the price goes negative

Why: this is the entire mechanism the unit explains — CI can only check what's already been thought to test.

items.prompt: According to L2's flowchart, when is CI "structurally blind" to a problem?
choices: When the change introduces a genuinely new scenario that existing checks don't cover
Whenever the build takes longer than five minutes
Whenever more than one file is changed in a PR
CI is never blind to any problem, by definition
items.explanation: CI's blindness is specific: it can only catch regressions against what's already tested — a genuinely new scenario has, by definition, nothing already checking it.
items.reference:
✅ CI catches — regressions in already-tested behavior
❌ CI is blind to — anything nobody wrote a check for yet

Why: this isn't a flaw in CI — it's the structural nature of what automated checks can do.

items.prompt: Does L2 present CI's blind spot to untested scenarios as a flaw or malfunction in CI?
choices: No — it's presented as the structural nature of what automated checks can do, not a bug or misconfiguration
Yes — L2 argues CI should be reconfigured to catch every possible scenario
Yes — L2 argues CI is fundamentally unreliable and should be removed
L2 doesn't address whether this is a flaw or not
items.explanation: L2 (and L3) are explicit that CI passing on the buggy PR isn't CI malfunctioning — it's checking exactly what it was configured to check, correctly, and that set simply didn't include the new scenario.
items.reference:
✅ CI catches — regressions in already-tested behavior
❌ CI is blind to — anything nobody wrote a check for yet

Why: this isn't a flaw in CI — it's the structural nature of what automated checks can do.

items.prompt: According to L2's table, what should a reviewer spend their limited attention on, given that CI already handles regressions?
choices: Missing test coverage, design issues, and "what about X?" questions — territory CI structurally can't cover
Re-verifying that the build succeeded, since CI results can't be trusted
Counting the number of lines changed in the PR
Checking that the PR was opened during business hours
items.explanation: L2 argues a reviewer's real value is in the territory CI can't cover — re-checking what CI already verified wastes the reviewer's limited, valuable attention.
items.reference:
CI gatingHuman review
CatchesRegressions in tested behaviorMissing coverage, design, edge cases

Why: a reviewer re-checking already-covered territory isn't adding value — it's duplicating CI's work while missing the questions only a human can ask.

items.prompt: Why does L2 say a reviewer who re-verifies things CI already checked is wasting attention?
choices: Because that territory is already covered — the reviewer's unique value is asking questions no automated check can ask on its own
Because CI results are usually wrong and shouldn't be trusted at all
Because reviewers are not allowed to look at test results
Because re-verification always takes longer than the original CI run
items.explanation: Since CI already reliably covers regression territory, a reviewer spending time there duplicates already-done work instead of applying the one kind of scrutiny only a human can provide.
items.reference:
CI gatingHuman review
CatchesRegressions in tested behaviorMissing coverage, design, edge cases

Why: a reviewer re-checking already-covered territory isn't adding value — it's duplicating CI's work while missing the questions only a human can ask.

items.prompt: In L2's blocking-check flowchart, what happens if CI's automated checks fail?
choices: The merge button is disabled — a hard gate, not a request
The PR is automatically deleted
The reviewer is notified but the merge proceeds anyway
The failing check is automatically skipped on the next attempt
items.explanation: The flowchart shows a failed check disabling the merge button entirely — this is the concrete mechanism behind "gating," as opposed to a check that just reports status.
items.reference:
1️⃣ PR opened
2️⃣ CI runs — fail → merge disabled
3️⃣ Review — changes requested → cycle repeats
4️⃣ Both pass → merge allowed

Why: the flowchart makes the gating mechanism concrete — a hard block, not a suggestion.

items.prompt: In L2's flowchart, does a PR need to pass CI before or after being reviewed?
choices: CI runs first — review happens after CI checks pass
Review always happens first, and CI runs only after approval
CI and review never both apply to the same PR
The order doesn't matter and is never specified
items.explanation: The flowchart places CI's automated checks before the reviewer's involvement — reviewers engage with a PR that's already passed the automated gate, not one that might still fail basic checks.
items.reference:
1️⃣ PR opened
2️⃣ CI runs — fail → merge disabled
3️⃣ Review — changes requested → cycle repeats
4️⃣ Both pass → merge allowed

Why: the flowchart makes the gating mechanism concrete — a hard block, not a suggestion.

items.prompt: L2's failure modes list warns against treating a green CI checkmark as "this PR is correct." What does a green checkmark actually confirm?
choices: Nothing already-tested broke — it says nothing about whether the change itself is the right one, or whether it's missing coverage for its own new behavior
That the code is bug-free and ready for production with no further review needed
That the PR author is a senior engineer
That the PR has been read and understood by at least one human
items.explanation: A passing CI run confirms only that existing, already-encoded checks still hold — it makes no claim about correctness of new behavior or coverage of new scenarios.
items.reference:
✅ Green checkmark — nothing already-tested broke
❓ Not confirmed — whether the new behavior itself is correct

Why: conflating "nothing regressed" with "this is correct" is exactly the mistake that let the discount bug through until a reviewer asked a question.

items.prompt: Why is it a mistake for a reviewer to skim and approve a PR purely because CI is green?
choices: Because CI's coverage and review's coverage are different territory — a passing suite says nothing about a scenario a new PR just made reachable
Because CI results are usually inaccurate and shouldn't be trusted
Because skimming is always faster than genuine review, which wastes company resources
Because green checkmarks are randomly assigned and don't reflect actual test results
items.explanation: This is exactly the opening scenario's mechanism — the discount PR was fully green, and only a reviewer's substantive question caught the actual bug CI structurally couldn't see.
items.reference:
✅ Green checkmark — nothing already-tested broke
❓ Not confirmed — whether the new behavior itself is correct

Why: conflating "nothing regressed" with "this is correct" is exactly the mistake that let the discount bug through until a reviewer asked a question.

items.prompt: L2's failure modes list warns against making review "purely a formality." What's the specific cost of a rubber-stamp approval?
choices: It provides none of review's actual value — it adds latency without adding the scrutiny it's supposed to provide
It makes CI run more slowly
It's technically impossible to configure in most PR tools
It automatically fails CI for unrelated reasons
items.explanation: A rubber-stamp review still takes time (latency) but delivers none of the actual benefit — the worst combination, since it looks like scrutiny happened when it didn't.
items.reference:
⏱️ Rubber-stamp review — adds delay
🚫 Provides — none of review's actual scrutiny

Why: a review process that looks rigorous on paper but isn't in practice is arguably worse than no review policy at all, since it creates false confidence.

items.prompt: Why might a rubber-stamp review culture be worse than having no formal review requirement at all?
choices: It creates false confidence — a team believes its PRs are being scrutinized when they're actually not, which is more dangerous than knowing scrutiny is missing
It's always slower than having no review process
It costs more money in tooling licenses
It's identical in every way to having no review requirement
items.explanation: A visible "approved" status implies real scrutiny happened — when it didn't, the team has a false sense of security about exactly the bugs review is meant to catch.
items.reference:
⏱️ Rubber-stamp review — adds delay
🚫 Provides — none of review's actual scrutiny

Why: a review process that looks rigorous on paper but isn't in practice is arguably worse than no review policy at all, since it creates false confidence.

items.prompt: Implement `applyDiscountFixed(price, discountPercent)`. Clamp `discountPercent` to the range [0, 100] before applying it — a value above 100 should behave as if it were exactly 100 (price becomes 0), and a negative value should behave as if it were exactly 0 (price is unchanged). Round the result to 2 decimal places using `Math.round(n * 100) / 100`.

tests.description: a combined discount over 100% clamps to a price of 0, not negative
a negative discount clamps to 0, leaving the price unchanged
a discount of exactly 0 leaves the price unchanged

items.explanation: Math.min(100, Math.max(0, discountPercent)) clamps the input into [0, 100] before it's ever used in the price calculation, so no combination of stacked discounts can push the result below 0 or above the original price. This is exactly L3's fix for the discount-stacking bug the reviewer caught, node-verified against the original bug's exact numbers.
items.reference:
❌ Buggy — no clamp, 110% discount produces a negative price
✅ Fixed — Math.min/Math.max clamps to [0, 100] first

Why: this is the exact fix the reviewer's question led to in L3 — verified against the same 60%+50% combined-discount scenario from the opening story.

tests.description: a combined markdown over 100% clamps to a price of 0, not negative

a markdown of exactly 0 leaves the price unchanged

items.explanation: Math.min(100, Math.max(0, markdownPercent)) clamps the input into [0, 100] before it's ever used in the price calculation, so no combination of stacked markdowns can push the result below 0 or above the original price — the same clamping pattern as applyDiscountFixed, applied to differently-named inputs.
items.reference:

items.prompt: Implement `combineDiscounts(percentages)`. Sum the array of percentages, then clamp the total to the range [0, 100] (a sum above 100 becomes 100; a sum below 0 becomes 0). An empty array should return 0.

tests.description: combining two normal discounts sums them correctly
combining discounts that exceed 100% clamps the total to 100
an empty array of discounts returns 0

items.explanation: Summing the array first, then clamping the total to [0, 100] with a single Math.min/Math.max pair, correctly caps any combination of stacked discounts — this is exactly the bug L3's opening scenario surfaced: computeCombinedDiscount(60, 50) producing 110 with nothing capping it before being passed to applyDiscount.
items.reference:
➕ Sum first — total every stacked discount
🔒 Clamp once — cap the total to [0, 100], not each individual discount

Why: clamping the combined total (not each input separately) is what actually prevents the opening scenario's 60% + 50% = 110% bug.

items.prompt: In L3's reverse case (the function rename), why couldn't the reviewer be expected to catch the broken call site in `invoicing.js`?
choices: Because a reviewer reading only the changed lines in the PR's diff has no reason to know invoicing.js exists or calls the renamed function
Because reviewers are not allowed to look at more than one file
Because invoicing.js was intentionally hidden from the review tool
Because the reviewer was on vacation during this PR
items.explanation: The diff shown to the reviewer only includes the changed file — a call site in a completely different, unchanged file simply isn't part of what a diff-focused review would ever look at.
items.reference:
📄 Diff shown — one file, one obvious call site updated
📄 Not shown — invoicing.js, a different file, still using the old name

Why: this is the mirror image of the discount bug — here, CI's exhaustive full-suite run is what catches what review structurally can't.

items.prompt: What specifically catches the broken call site in L3's reverse case, and why?
choices: CI's full test suite, because it runs the entire codebase (including invoicing.js's tests) every time, not just the changed files
The reviewer, because they eventually noticed it on a second read
Nothing catches it — the bug ships to production undetected
The PR's title, which flags renamed functions automatically
items.explanation: CI's advantage here is exhaustiveness — it runs every test in the codebase, including ones for files the diff never shows, so a broken call site anywhere fails immediately.
items.reference:
📄 Diff shown — one file, one obvious call site updated
📄 Not shown — invoicing.js, a different file, still using the old name

Why: this is the mirror image of the discount bug — here, CI's exhaustive full-suite run is what catches what review structurally can't.

items.prompt: L3's extend-it question asks what category of bug neither CI nor a normal diff-focused review would catch. What kind of bug fits that description?
choices: Something that only shows up under real production traffic or real data — like a race condition that only occurs under concurrent load neither tests nor a reviewer's reasoning reliably reproduces
A typo in a variable name, since typos are always caught by every tool
A missing semicolon, since linters always catch syntax issues
Any bug at all — CI and review together catch 100% of possible bugs
items.explanation: Bugs that depend on real-world conditions (production load, real data distributions, timing) are the category L3 flags as a genuine gap — neither a test suite's fixed scenarios nor a reviewer's reasoning about the diff reliably surfaces them.
items.reference:
✅ CI catches — regressions in tested behavior
✅ Review catches — untested new scenarios, reasoned about
❓ Neither catches — bugs that only appear under real production conditions

Why: this is L3's own extend-it question — an honest acknowledgment that the two-mechanism model in this unit has a real, open gap.

items.prompt: Why does L3 frame the production-only bug category as "a real, open gap" rather than something PRs and CI should be expected to fully solve?
choices: Because PRs and CI are structurally limited to what's reasoned about or already tested before the change ships — some bugs are only observable once real conditions exist
Because PRs and CI are outdated practices that should be abandoned
Because this category of bug doesn't actually exist in real systems
Because only production incidents matter, making PRs and CI unnecessary
items.explanation: L3 is honest that PRs and CI operate entirely before a change reaches real conditions — some bugs are fundamentally about what happens under real traffic or real data, which no pre-merge process can fully simulate.
items.reference:
✅ CI catches — regressions in tested behavior
✅ Review catches — untested new scenarios, reasoned about
❓ Neither catches — bugs that only appear under real production conditions

Why: this is L3's own extend-it question — an honest acknowledgment that the two-mechanism model in this unit has a real, open gap.
